name: Assessing Learning When Students Have AI
title: Assessing Learning When Students Have AI
answer: AI has changed what some assessments can tell teachers, because a take home essay or problem set may now show what a tool can do rather than what a student can do. The response is to design assessments that reveal what students themselves know, using in class work, drafts with version history, and short conversations about the work. Some tasks can also invite AI openly, asking students to generate a first answer and then critique and improve it.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Assessment design has to answer a question that AI has made harder, which is whether a piece of submitted work reflects the student or the tool. A take home essay or problem set that once served as proof of learning may no longer do so. The book treats this as a design problem rather than a policing problem, and it connects the answer to the same thinking about building integrity through process that it applied earlier. Teachers need assessments that show what students themselves know, and that means choosing formats deliberately rather than keeping old ones by default. The idea is to sort assessments into those that still work, those that need changing, and those that should include AI openly.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In class writing and problem solving show what students can do on their own, drafts with version history show how a piece of work developed, and short conversations in which students explain their work reveal whether they understand it. Other assessments can include AI on purpose, for example a task that asks students to use AI to generate a first answer and then critique and improve it while showing their reasoning at each step. That kind of task measures skills students will need, such as judging AI output. The AI use levels described earlier in the book give teachers a way to label what is allowed on each assessment. The supplied text does not break these approaches down by grade band, so the choice of format is left to the teacher or the team.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text offers no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it offers instead is a design argument, that a take home essay or problem set may now reflect what a tool can do rather than what a student can do. The approaches it recommends, such as in class work, version history and explanation conversations, are presented as things that help rather than as findings from a trial. Readers should treat the idea as a practical response to a changed condition, not as a claim backed by measured results.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text keeps the important decisions with people. A department, not a tool, reviews its major assessments and decides which ones still work, which need changes, and which should include AI openly, and the team decides what each assessment is meant to measure. AI can help draft revised tasks and rubrics, but that is assistance with drafting rather than a decision about purpose. The risk the text names is that an assessment stops showing what a student can do, which is why formats such as in class work and explanation conversations matter. Nothing in the text sets out rules or limits beyond this, and the judgement about what any given assessment is for stays with the teacher or team.
